claims.text: FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles have equilibrium atomic distributions in their as-synthesized state.
Replica Exchange Molecular Dynamics or metadynamics can be integrated with standard molecular dynamics to study FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles across multiple sizes.
Free-energy barrier heights control melting and structural-transition processes in these nanoparticles.
The free-energy landscape mediates the thermal stability of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Enhanced sampling techniques overcome free-energy barriers more efficiently than conventional molecular dynamics.
Enhanced sampling permits detection of size-dependent shifts in the free-energy landscape.
Increased surface-to-volume effects in smaller nanoparticles cause size-dependent shifts in the free-energy landscape.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower free-energy barriers for melting than larger particles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower free-energy barriers for structural transitions than larger particles.
Reduced free-energy barriers for melting and structural transitions produce lower thermal stability.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower melting temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Conventional molecular dynamics inadequately captures free-energy barriers in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Conventional molecular dynamics inadequately captures finite-size effects in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The magnitude of the predicted barrier reduction and melting-temperature decrease depends on simulation parameters.
Interatomic-potential accuracy can influence the observed size-dependent thermal trends.
Simulation timescale can influence the observed size-dependent thermal trends.
